Q: Zip arrays in JavaScript? A:

There will be dedicated function in the near future! There is stage 3 draft of Iterator.zip() function which do exactly what you want:

const a = [1, 2, 3]
const b = ["a", "b", "c"]

Iterator.zip(a, b).toArray();

// > [[1, "a"], [2, "b"], [3, "c"]]

link to MDN (docs). At the bottom of the page you can see current adoption and links to polyfills that already implement it (core-js, es-shims)

The draft also define Iterator.zipKeyed() which work similarly but outputs objects instead of lists.

Q: Looking for App Feature Ideas Aligned with My Travel & Tour Business A:

Such a post doesn't belong on StackOverflow, and is more at home elsewhere (maybe Reddit). SO is more for specific technical questions and answers.

Anyways, my comments for you:

1. Core features: Why are you asking that here? That is something you should ask your customers and colleagues. As well, simply spend some hours observing other travel apps and websites will give you all your answers. Ask AI too, of course.

2. Mobile app: It seems early for you to be making this choice; front-ends can come-and-go. Since you're an information based app, and not a heavy game or something, then cross-platform frameworks make sense. If you're considering Flutter and React Native, maybe take a glance at Ionic Capacitor; I have published apps on app stores with this. They had one codebase powering everything: website, iOS and Android.

3. Backend: Excluding bookings for a moment, for general business purposes I'd imagine you'd have a CMS/CRM using some kind of framework for that (Sanity, Strapi or 20 other candidates) holding most of your records. I've built a few CMS instances for businesses and have often used Strapi's free community version. Often in this context WordPress (another CMS) is used but personally I would avoid it like the plague. You could keep bookings in the same system but personally I would run a completely separate custom project and server, a custom booking engine with whatever-mainstream-language-you-or-your-devs-prefer. For DB, yes probably PostgreSQL all round and personally I'd have bookings with it's own DB. A basic auth layer usually comes along with the CMS/CRM but you could use yet another service for this too.

4. APIs: Not sure what you mean - Are you asking what payment platforms and map platforms you'd leverage? For payments, this is more of a business question; all of the major payment platforms have APIs you'll integrate with. I would be looking at what payment platform can handle the payment types and customers types you have. In North America, you would look at stuff like Stripe or Square or 20 others. I have no idea about Phillipines. As for maps, do you mean what map technology is best for users in your front-end? I mean invariably Google Maps is the best. Or are you talking about path-finding features like a rideshare app has?

5. Data design: This is asking for quite a bit of hand-holding. I will say you are on the right track in that you will have data types for various things (everything!). If you're leveraging a CMS/CRM framework (as mentioned earlier), simply building up content types in the respective dashboard is all you need to do, and these will evolve over time. Focus on the business needs, the fields, the relations. Don't sweat SQL columns yourself in the early prototyping phase, but keep in mind scrutinizing this with an expert before committing to a million records.

---

Instead of trying to do all at once, consider these paradigms: Front-end driven development (FEDD) vs Back-end driven development (BEDD). Google it. There's advantages/disadvantages. If you have a strong UX/UI designer with you for the long run, FEDD makes some sense. Otherwise, my opinion is it's best for you to become intimate with the back-end as it's more crucial to business needs. Front-end can be tackled in parallel and in isolation and you can hire one-off contractors for it.

Here's another perspective:

THERE'S LOTS OF "FRONT-ENDS": Ways customers could interact with you: Website, Mobile app, Facebook, Instagram, Tiktok, Whatsapp, Direct messaging, Email, Phone, In-person, etc.

Currently you already have front-ends, and they have nothing to interact with.

ONLY ONE "BACK-END": You have no back-end yet, and there's no alternative; you must have a back-end.

Q: Might there be problems with using "get" to modify a the value of the property? A:

First, there seems no run-time/semantic reason in using a getter in this circumstance for setActive or setInactive. It's just the syntactic change of the missing parenthesis when invoked.

And if this is an API, it would be advisable to get its users what they are expecting. I for one, if I see a verb there in the name of the property like "setActive" I would see it as a function, and my "muscle memory" would most likely add the parenthesis, or I would think the documentation has a typo (missing parenthesis). Even after I get the error "obj.setActive" is not a function, I would find it unpleasant each time I'd have to enter it without the parenthesis (and possibly emit an unkind thought towards the person who did that to me).

Q: Google Sheets - 2D Lookup Returning the Associated Column Header Within an Array Formula A:

try:

=INDEX(IFERROR(VLOOKUP(B2:INDEX(B:B, MAX((B:B<>"")*ROW(B:B))), 
 SPLIT(TOCOL(D2:Z&"×"&D1:Z1), "×"), 2, 0), "invalid"))

if you want to use your formula you should try BYROW like:

=BYROW(B2:INDEX(B:B, MAX((B:B<>"")*ROW(B:B))), LAMBDA(b, IFERROR(IFS(ISBLANK(b), "", 
 COUNTIF(INDIRECT("D2:Z1000"), b) = 0, "Invalid", 
 COUNTIF(INDIRECT("B2:B"), b) > 1, "Duplicate", LEN(b), 
 HLOOKUP(1, {SORTN(SEARCH(b, INDIRECT("D2:Z1000"))); INDIRECT("D1:Z1")}, 2, )), "Invalid")))

Q: Should my project's CMakeLists create a target export file in the build dir and the package registry? A:

No, targets should not generally be consumed from build trees which is what export() exists to support. The CMake documentation gives the canonical use-case for export().

Creates a file <filename> that may be included by outside projects to import targets named by <target>... from the current project's build tree. This is useful during cross-compiling to build utility executables that can run on the host platform in one project and then import them into another project being compiled for the target platform.

If you're not doing something akin to this use case, exporting utilities to be used by other build trees (typically in the same source repo), you shouldn't be using export().
